name: Elena Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in my first year of a secondary maths teaching degree. Mornings are lectures in pure maths and education theory, afternoons are problem sets in the library, and two evenings a week I work at a bakery on Cross Street, shaping rolls from four to nine. I live with my aunt Marisol because my parents are overseas and can't help with money. I won a scholarship place, and I want to be the maths teacher I wish I'd had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a normal ups-and-downs thing. AI will help with marking and lesson plans, and that's useful, but teaching is about the room, not the paperwork. Most of my friends are in courses that look more exposed than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine about the job and tight about the money. Teacher pay is okay but not great, and my loan is going to be large by the time I start. Plateau means the same world, and that's one where I'd be paying off the loan for about twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the bakery shifts, work on my grades and try some AI marking tools on my own practice papers. I'd ask the school-placement office about paid tutoring. And I'd put a little aside each month for my own books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit tired, but good. I like knowing where I'm headed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you live with your aunt. What would change if the bakery shifts stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be short on the money for my aunt's rent contribution, and I'd have to ask her to wait. She never asks for it, which makes me feel worse. I'd pick up weekend tutoring for pocket money, which beats rolling bread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend about teaching as a career in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That teaching is a good job if you like people. It's not rich, but it's stable and nobody is going to remove the teacher from the classroom soon. Parents want a person who knows their child.

say: I'd say AI helps with **marking** and lesson plans, but teaching is about the room.
I'd say most friends' courses look more **exposed** than mine.
think: Privately, I'm fine about the job and tight about **money**.
My loan will be large, and I'd be paying it off for about **twenty** years.
do: Keep the **bakery** shifts and try AI marking tools on my own practice papers.
Ask the placement office about paid **tutoring**.
feel: **Okay**; tired but good, since I know where I'm headed.
S0.quote: Teaching is a good job if you like people. It's not rich, but it's stable and nobody is going to remove the teacher from the classroom soon.
fieldNote: She is steady about the **job** and tight about money, with parents overseas who cannot help.
Tries AI once it is proven useful, and looks for tutoring as a better-paid side job.

steps.text: Keep the two weekly evening shifts at the bakery
Ask the placement office about paid tutoring work
Try an AI marking tool on practice papers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the paperwork goes first: marking, reports, lesson plans, emails to parents. That's where most teachers lose their evenings. I'd say it gives us time back, if schools let us keep it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit nervous, because schools could use AI as a reason to cut support staff. And if one AI tutor does what three did, there might be fewer jobs for new teachers. But I think good teachers are still wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly in my second year, because I'd rather know them than be told how to use them. I'd keep the bakery for now, and add a maths tutoring side job. I'd ask my lecturers how schools are changing their hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously okay. I'm a bit wary, but it doesn't feel like the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What parts of a teacher's day do you think software takes over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably be okay with AI tutors for practice drills. The question is who watches the kids who zone out, or who are having a bad week at home. A machine can't be there for a kid who's having a bad week at home. That's the human bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about a classroom with AI tutors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay and the number of jobs. If schools get the same funding and use AI to do more with fewer staff, new teachers like me would find fewer posts. I'd have to be flexible about where I work.

say: I'd say the **paperwork** goes first, and it gives teachers time back if schools let us keep it.
I'd say good teachers will still be **wanted**.
think: Privately, I'm **nervous** that schools could cut support staff and hire fewer new teachers.
I'd feel better knowing the **tools** properly.
do: Learn the **tools** properly in second year and add a maths tutoring side job.
Ask my **lecturers** how schools are changing their hiring.
feel: **Cautiously** okay; wary, but it doesn't feel like the end.
S1.quote: A machine can't be there for a kid who's having a bad week at home. That's the human bit.
fieldNote: She expects **fewer** new-teacher posts if schools use AI to save money, and plans for flexibility.
Steady temperament: learns the tools once proven and keeps a side income.

steps.text: Learn AI lesson-planning tools properly in second year
Start maths tutoring on weekends for pocket money
Ask lecturers how schools are changing hiring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and it needs a government response. I'd say teachers will still matter, but nobody knows how. I'd probably say less online and more at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared. In two years I'm barely done with my first year of teaching practice, and AI could do most thinking jobs, including the planning part of teaching. Robots for hands-on work come around 2031, so classrooms might change a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the degree because I don't know a better plan. I'd work extra shifts at the bakery to save, and look at a second subject like computing in case I need a different route. I'd also write my parents a long letter, because it's hard to say on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty shaken. I'd feel like I'm steering a boat in fog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month after hearing it was two years away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents that I'm okay, but that I might need help one day. They'd say come home, and I'd say I can't. It's a hard conversation, because they're sacrificing already and I don't want to be another worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents overseas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt Marisol. She's got her own bills, and if I lose a year to a bad job market I'd be leaning on her more. I'd rather lose a year of sleep than be a weight on my aunt.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and needs a government response.
I'd say teachers will still matter, but nobody knows **how**.
think: Privately, I'd be **scared**: AI could do the planning half of teaching within two years.
I'd feel like I'm steering a boat in **fog**.
do: Stay in the degree, work extra **bakery** shifts and look at a second subject like computing.
Write my **parents** a long letter, because it's hard on the phone.
feel: **Shaken**, like steering a boat in fog.
S2.quote: I'd rather lose a year of sleep than be a weight on my aunt.
fieldNote: The hardest part is **family**: parents overseas already sacrificing, and an aunt with her own bills.
She hedges by adding a second subject rather than leaving teaching.

steps.text: Work extra bakery shifts to build a small cushion
Look into a second subject like computing
Stay in the teaching degree and keep studying
Write my parents a letter explaining my plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still fast, but there's a window. I'd say schools and unis need to plan now, and teachers should be part of the plan, not told afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be uneasy but not panicked. I'd graduate in three years, teach for two before robots come, and have a profession that people trust. I'd have to be adaptable, but I think I'd get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, get a teaching placement in a school that uses the new tools and keep up the bakery job for the money. I'd save about forty pounds a month for a safety fund. And I'd talk to older teachers about what they're seeing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little better. It's the kind of worry that gets me to plan, not freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives a bit more time. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be worrying less about the first year and more about the long run: what do schools look like in 2034? I'd say I want to be one of the teachers who knows the tools, and who understands how kids learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change for you compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt would get older and I'd want to help her, not the other way round. Five years gives me a bit of time to get a job and start paying my aunt back. That matters more than the robots to me.

say: I'd say there's a **window**, and teachers should be part of the plan, not told afterwards.
I'd say schools and unis need to plan **now**.
think: Privately, I'd be **uneasy** but not panicked: I'd teach for two years before robots come.
do: Finish the degree and take a placement in a school using the new **tools**.
Save forty pounds a month for a **safety** fund and talk to older teachers.
feel: A little **better**; a worry that gets me to plan, not freeze.
S3.quote: Five years gives me a bit of time to get a job and start paying my aunt back.
fieldNote: The longer **window** turns her fear into planning; she wants to be the teacher who knows the tools.
Her loyalty to her **aunt** matters more to her than the robots.

steps.text: Take a teaching placement in a school using new tools
Save forty pounds a month in a safety fund
Talk to older teachers about what they are seeing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade to get things right. Teachers, parents and councils should use the time to rethink what schools are for. I'd be an advocate for keeping teachers at the centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel good. I'd qualify, teach for about six years and build up a reputation. I might become a head of maths. The robots in classrooms would come after I've had a proper career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take my first job, and start paying the loan down. I'd move into my own flat after two years. And I'd do a masters in education part time, because that's how you move up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. I'd have time to enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what changes about your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry that nobody plans for it, and schools end up scrambling in year nine. I'd also worry that kids from poorer homes get machines while richer kids get teachers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' health, because I haven't seen them in two years. A decade gives me time to bring them over, if I can afford it. That's a plan I'd love to make real.

say: I'd say a decade is long enough to **rethink** what schools are for, with teachers at the centre.
I'd advocate for keeping **teachers** in the room.
think: Privately, I'd feel **good**: qualify, teach for six years and maybe lead the maths department.
Classroom robots would come after I've had a proper **career**.
do: Finish the degree, take my first **job** and start paying the loan down.
Do a part-time **masters** in education and move into my own flat.
feel: Fairly **calm**, with time to enjoy it.
S4.quote: I'd also worry that kids from poorer homes get machines while richer kids get teachers.
fieldNote: A decade lets her picture a real **career**, a flat and bringing her parents over.
Her concern is **fairness** for pupils, not her own job.

steps.text: Finish the degree and start teaching maths
Pay the student loan down steadily
Study a part-time masters in education

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened? And is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'd have barely started, and my aunt and my parents would all be looking at me. What would help is a government that gives teachers notice and retraining, and a loan that doesn't follow you if the job disappears. One thing you didn't ask: I picked teaching because I was a quiet kid and one teacher noticed me. I'd hate to think that's something a machine could do.

headlineQuote: I picked teaching because I was a quiet kid and one teacher noticed me.
portrait: Elena is a first-year **maths teaching** student who lives with her aunt Marisol and bakes rolls on two evenings a week.
Her parents are overseas and cannot help, so **money** is tight and she carries a scholarship's pressure.
Centre and steady, she tries tools once they are **proven** and always keeps a plan B.
Her calm in slow worlds becomes **alarm** when two years would leave her unfinished and her family leaning on her.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case worries her most: barely started, with her aunt and parents depending on her.
whatWouldHelp: Notice and **retraining** for teachers, and a loan that does not follow you if the job disappears.
